messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Ways to reduce graininess in spectrogram plots?
messages.subject_clean: [seewave] Ways to reduce graininess in spectrogram plots?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sean,

Have you considered changing your collevels? It looks like you're binning the levels into 0.5 dB bins, which might create the illusion of graininess. On the other hand, if you find that the labels and axes numbering are also grainy (pixelated?), then it's as Jerome suggested: you need to save the image at a higher resolution.

If you're saving with the png() function, try increasing the res to 300 or more. If you're using the built-in Rstudio Export, it doesn't have a dpi/res option, so I would explore png().

Steffi

University of Northern BC

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Automatically detect bird sound
messages.body_plain:
Dear ??,

The function to do automatic detection is timer() but it is based on a rather simple threshold principle and will probably be difficult to handle with so large files.
Another solution could be to have a look at the package monitoR that processes automatic identification based on template matching.
Best
Jerome

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] general question about entropy
messages.body_plain:
Dear Sean,

It is not a seewave question but I will try to reply quickly.

In the original paper where we described the entopy-like indices, we referred to two indices: (1) H[t] deals with the PMF of the amplitude envelope, and (2) H[f] deals with the PMF of the (mean) frequency spectrum.

A pure tone with a square amplitude envelope will return a high H[t] but a low H[f] because the envelope is flat but the frequency spectrum is characterised by a unique frequency peak.
A white noise will have a high H[t] and high H[f] because both envelope and frequency spectrum tend to be flat.

The index H, which multiplies H[t] and H[f], can therefore return mixed results depending on both envelope and spectrum shapes.

HTH a bit,

Jerome

De: "Sean Hardison" <seanha...@gmail.com>
À: "seewave GROUP" <see...@googlegroups.com>
Envoyé: Jeudi 20 Octobre 2016 17:55:10
Objet: [seewave] general question about entropy

Hi everybody,

My understanding of entropy is that it's the uncertainty in a scenario, so if there are equal chances of an outcome occurring, entropy is at its maximum because there's no way we could predict an outcome. Following this logic, why is it that noisy signals trend higher in the acoustic entropy index compared to simpler waveforms? If I plot the PMF of the amplitude for a simple sine wave, it looks like there is a relatively equal probability of any one amplitude occurring. Can someone explain to me what I'm missing?

Thanks

Sean

--
